unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 9: Amazing Arts — the final unit of Year 6! In this unit you will explore how art, music, and creative expression can transform communities and inspire change. You will read about children who turn broken objects into beautiful instruments, empty walls into colourful murals, and dusty valleys into thriving green spaces. Through these stories and activities, you will sharpen your English skills and discover the power of creativity.
unit.learningPath:
Start with the Vocabulary file and learn a few words each day, adding them to your Word Wall.
Work through the grammar lessons: indefinite pronouns, adjective order, and the present perfect review.
Read "The Children of Wind Valley" and "The Mural Makers" reading, then answer the comprehension questions.
Complete the speaking, writing and activity tasks in this lesson file in order.
Finish with the unit quiz and the Check Your Learning self-assessment.

readings.title: How Art Transforms a Community
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
Art, music and creative expression can transform communities and inspire change. To transform something is to change its form so completely that it becomes something new — and all over East Africa, young people are proving that a paintbrush, a drum or a packet of seeds can do exactly that.
In one town, children turned broken objects into beautiful instruments: an old oil tin became a drum, a bicycle wheel became a rattle, and a length of pipe became a flute. In another, teenagers turned empty grey walls into colourful murals of hills, animals and planted trees. In a third, a whole village turned a dusty valley into a thriving green space by planting and watering, week after week, until the ground flourished.
None of these projects began with money. They began with someone who noticed a problem and imagined something better, and with the willingness to keep going when the first attempt failed. Creativity, it turns out, is not only about talent. It is about looking at what everyone else has walked past and asking, "What could this become?"
When a place changes, the people in it change too. A street with a mural feels safer and friendlier. A school with a band has children who arrive early to practise. A green valley gives a village shade, food and pride. That is what it means to say that art transforms communities: it does not only decorate them, it helps them grow.

readings.title: The Mural Makers of Mogadishu
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
In many cities around the world, art has the power to transform empty spaces into places of hope and beauty. One of the most exciting examples of this comes from communities where young people pick up paintbrushes instead of waiting for change to arrive. They decide that everyone deserves to see colour and creativity in their daily lives — and they make it happen themselves.
In a neighbourhood on the outskirts of a large East African city, a group of teenagers noticed that the walls along the main road were cracked, grey, and covered in dust. Nothing about the street felt welcoming. Families walked past quickly, and children had nowhere special to play. The teenagers decided to change that. They formed a group called the Mural Makers.
The Mural Makers began by collecting leftover paint from local shops and workshops. Someone donated old brushes. Anyone who wanted to help was welcome, and soon the group grew to more than thirty young artists. They did not need expensive equipment or access to a fancy studio. All they needed was a wall, a plan, and the commitment to finish what they started.
Their first project was a mural on the side of a community hall. Zara, the group’s leader, sketched the design in her notebook using neat cursive handwriting. The mural showed a landscape of green hills, a bright sun, and children planting trees together. “We want people to see what this place could look like,” Zara explained. “Art helps us imagine a better future.”
The teenagers learned to organise their adjectives carefully when describing their supplies. They asked for “a large rectangular wooden board” to mix paint on, and they described their finished mural as “a beautiful tall colourful East African scene.” This kind of careful adjective order made their English writing sound natural and polished.
Slowly, the neighbourhood began to change. Where there had been bare walls, there were now bright images of animals, flowers, and famous East African landscapes. An old man who had lived on the street for decades said, “Everything looks different now. I feel proud of where I live.”

readings.title: The Children of Wind Valley, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
The village of Lusinga rested in a wide valley surrounded by high ridges and evergreen trees. It was once famous for its cool climate, its wildflowers, and the strong winds that whispered through the hills. But recently, the land had begun to suffer.
"There used to be so many trees here," said Amara, age 13, as she climbed a slope with her twin brother, Kofi. "Now look at this mess."
The mountain landscape was dry. Broken stumps replaced the old forest trails. Empty cans and torn plastic hung on the fallen branches. People had cleared much of the forest for firewood and farming. It was called deforestation, and it had changed everything.
"Even the wind feels wrong," said Kofi. "It is hotter now. The streams have dried up. And the peppermint plants are gone."
They sat on a rock overlooking the valley.
"We need to do something," Amara said.
At school the next day, their science teacher announced a project. "You will design a plan to help the environment," she said. "This region has suffered. Now it is your turn to help it recover."
"What can we do?" asked a boy.
"That is for you to analyse," she replied. "It may involve new tools, new rules, or even a new way of thinking."
The students were excited. Amara and Kofi formed a group with their classmates Imani and Tariq. They named their group The Children of Wind Valley.
The first thing they did was research. "We have already lost sixty per cent of our forest," said Imani, reading aloud. "Many animals have relocated. The soil is dry. And we have had more floods this year than ever before."
Kofi pointed at a graph. "Temperatures have climbed, too. This valley used to be cooler. Now it is close to the subtropics."
Tariq nodded. "My grandmother says the wind used to sing. Now it screams."
They decided on a goal: to preserve what was left and replant what had been lost. They made posters and maps, and Tariq wrote all their titles in neat cursive. One poster said: "Plant. Protect. Pass it on." Imani added a caption: "Wind Valley is our heritage. Nature is not just space; it is memory."
They visited a local farm with a wind turbine, and the farmer explained how it worked. "The turbine collects the wind's power and turns it into electricity," he said.
"Could we build a small one at school?" Kofi asked.
"With the right support," the farmer replied. "You would need planning, commitment, and money."
The team met under the big fig tree after school. Imani held up a drawing. "Imagine it," she said. "A small wind farm. A tree nursery. A learning centre."
"It will take real sacrifice," said Amara. "Time, energy, and patience. Maybe some people will not like it."

readings.title: The Children of Wind Valley, part 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
"But it could be a model for other schools," said Tariq. "A thriving space for nature and learning." They called it the Ridge Replanting Project.
They wrote a proposal using the present perfect: "We have measured changes in temperature and soil quality. We have mapped the affected zones. We have spoken to local farmers and elders."
They practised the future tense too: "We will plant one hundred trees. We will build a wind model. We will create a new environmental club."
They used clear adjective order as well, describing "a small wooden solar-powered nursery" and "a wide circular concrete platform."
Not everyone supported them. "This is just school talk," said a shopkeeper. "It is not real." One man shouted, "Stop blaming us for cutting trees! Do you want us to starve?" Some accused the group of trying to overthrow tradition.
"That is not our goal," Amara said in a public meeting. "We are not blaming. We are planting. Not to destroy the past, but to protect the future."
The district officer, Ms. Alina, came to their school. "I have read your proposal," she said. "It is detailed and powerful, especially your section on reform." She showed them her notes. "You have used real data, honest writing, and a clear vision."
"Will we get support?" Amara asked.
"You have earned a pilot grant," she said. "It is enough for fifty seedlings and a model turbine. But you must monitor everything and report each week."
They were amazed. "We did it!" said Imani.
That weekend, they began planting. Students dug holes and elders helped carry compost. A local artist painted a sign: "This ridge is a pluralistic place, where animals, trees, and children all belong."
They cleaned an old storehouse and turned it into a learning room, which they called The Green Room. Inside, Amara taped a sign on the wall: "We have sacrificed comfort for hope. We have collided with doubt. But this is our space of transformation."
By the end of the term, forty-seven trees had survived. Bees returned. Butterflies fluttered near the new flowers. Some peppermint bushes sprouted again.
The school held an open day. Visitors toured the ridge and the Green Room, and many said it was beautiful. Occasionally, someone still called it "just a school project."
Then a letter arrived, from a school in Rwanda: "We heard about your work. Could you send us your report? We want to start something too."
In the final assembly, the principal read from their first submission: "We believe in caring for the environment through education and respect. The wind has shaped our stories. Now we shape the wind."
Outside, the wind turned again, this time softer. The trees moved gently, and the ridge whispered. Amara smiled. "They said we could not change anything," she said. "And yet," said Kofi, "we have changed everything."

grammar.title: Indefinite Pronouns — The Basics
grammar.explanation: Indefinite pronouns are words that replace nouns without saying exactly who or what they refer to. They let us talk about people, things, or places in a general way. For example, instead of naming a specific person, you can say someone. Instead of listing every object, you can say everything. This is very useful in both speaking and writing.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
The four groups:
Indefinite pronouns come in four families. Each family has words for people, things, and places:
When to use each group:
some- words are used in positive statements and offers: "Someone left a gift on the desk." / "Would you like something to drink?"
any- words are used in questions and negative sentences: "Does anyone have a pencil?" / "I do not have anything to wear."
every- words mean ALL people, things, or places: "Everyone enjoyed the show." / "She looked everywhere."
no- words mean ZERO — none at all: "Nobody was late today." / "There is nothing left to eat."
The singular verb rule:
All indefinite pronouns that end in -one, -body, or -thing are singular. They take a singular verb:
Everyone is here. (not "Everyone are here.")
Nobody wants to leave. (not "Nobody want to leave.")
Something smells wonderful.
Nothing has changed.
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often make an indefinite pronoun plural, writing "Everyone are happy" or "Nobody know the answer." Words ending in -one, -body or -thing are singular, so the verb must be singular: "Everyone is happy."
grammar.memoryTip: "Indefinite" means "not definite." When you cannot point to the exact person or thing, reach for a some-, any-, every- or no- word and keep the verb singular.
grammar.practice:
Part A: fill each gap with someone, anyone, everyone, no one, something, nothing or everything. (1) ___ left a painting on the desk, but we do not know who. (2) Is ___ joining the art club? (3) ___ in the class enjoyed the concert. (4) There is ___ to fear, because we are ready. Part B: write two sentences of your own, one positive with a some- word and one negative with a no- word.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: (1) Someone (2) anyone (3) Everyone (4) nothing.
Part B: open-ended — self-check model: a positive sentence with a some- word, e.g. "Someone brought flowers for the classroom."; a negative sentence with a no- word, e.g. "Nobody wanted to leave early." Check that your some- sentence is positive and your no- sentence expresses zero/none.

grammar.title: Indefinite Pronouns — Advanced Uses
grammar.explanation: Now that you know the four groups, let us look at some more advanced rules. These will help you use indefinite pronouns like a confident English speaker.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Using they/their/them with indefinite pronouns:
In modern English, we often use they, their, and them to refer back to a singular indefinite pronoun when we do not know or do not want to specify the person's gender:
"Someone left their bag on the chair."
"Everyone should bring their own notebook."
"If anyone needs help, they can ask the teacher."
This is now accepted in standard English. It avoids the awkwardness of writing "his or her" every time.
Indefinite pronouns with adjectives:
When an adjective describes an indefinite pronoun, the adjective comes after the pronoun (not before):
"I want to eat something delicious." (not "delicious something")
"Is there anywhere quiet where I can study?" (not "quiet anywhere")
"We need someone brave to speak first." (not "brave someone")
Indefinite pronouns with else:
You can add else after an indefinite pronoun to mean "another" or "different":
"Is there anything else you need?"
"Someone else can take the lead today."
"Let us go somewhere else — this park is too crowded."
Double negatives — a trap to avoid:
In English, we do not use two negative words in the same clause:
Mistake: "I do not have nothing." ✗ (Two negatives cancel out.)
Fix: "I do not have anything." ✓ OR "I have nothing." ✓
grammar.commonMistake: A double negative cancels itself out. "I do not have nothing" really means you have something. Use one negative only: "I do not have anything" or "I have nothing."
grammar.memoryTip: An adjective follows the pronoun, not the other way round: say "something delicious" and "someone brave," and add "else" when you mean another one.

grammar.title: Adjective Order
grammar.explanation: In English, when we use more than one adjective before a noun, there is a natural order. If we put the adjectives in the wrong order, the sentence sounds odd to native speakers — even if the grammar is technically correct. Learning this order will make your writing sound polished and natural.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
The OSASCOMP order:
Use the word OSASCOMP to remember the standard order:
O — Opinion: beautiful, ugly, amazing, terrible, lovely
S — Size: big, small, tiny, enormous, tall, short
A — Age: old, new, young, ancient, modern
S — Shape: round, square, flat, rectangular, circular
C — Colour: red, blue, green, bright, dark, colourful
O — Origin: Somali, East African, British, Chinese, Kenyan
M — Material: wooden, metal, plastic, stone, glass, recycled
P — Purpose: cooking, sleeping, painting, writing, farming
Step-by-step guide:
When you have several adjectives, follow these steps:
Identify each adjective and its category (opinion, size, age, etc.).
Place them in the OSASCOMP order.
Check: does the phrase sound natural when you say it out loud?
Examples:
"a beautiful small old round bowl" — opinion + size + age + shape
"a large rectangular wooden board" — size + shape + material
"a lovely bright green Somali cloth" — opinion + colour + origin
"three tiny new circular metal trays" — quantity + size + age + shape + material
"a beautiful tall colourful East African scene" — opinion + size + colour + origin
grammar.commonMistake: Putting adjectives in the wrong order sounds odd. "A wooden large rectangular board" is wrong because material comes before size. Reorder as size, then shape, then material: "a large rectangular wooden board."
grammar.memoryTip: Remember OSASCOMP: Opinion, Size, Age, Shape, Colour, Origin, Material, Purpose. Opinion comes first and purpose comes last, right before the noun.
grammar.practice:

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: (1) a beautiful traditional Somali rug (opinion + style + origin) (2) a large new rectangular canvas (size + age + shape) (3) shiny tiny metal beads (opinion + size + material).
Part B: open-ended — self-check model: "I have a small wooden desk." (size + material) — check that your two adjectives follow the OSASCOMP order (Opinion, Size, Age, Shape, Colour, Origin, Material, Purpose).

grammar.title: Present Perfect Tense (Review)
grammar.explanation: The present perfect tense connects the past with the present. It tells us about actions that happened at some point in the past but are still relevant now. In the story "The Children of Wind Valley," the characters use the present perfect to show what they have already accomplished:
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
"We have measured changes in temperature."
"We have mapped the affected zones."
"We have spoken to local farmers."
How to form it:
Subject + have / has + past participle.
I / you / we / they + have + past participle: "We have planted fifty trees."
he / she / it + has + past participle: "She has inspired many people."
Negative: add not after have/has: "They have not finished yet." (or "haven't")
Question: put have/has before the subject: "Have you seen the new mural?"
Regular vs. irregular past participles
Regular: add -ed to the base verb: plant → planted, measure → measured, clean → cleaned.
Irregular: these must be memorised: go → gone, see → seen, build → built, speak → spoken, write → written, give → given, take → taken, make → made.
When to use the present perfect:
For experiences: "I have visited three countries."
For achievements: "She has written a beautiful poem."
For changes over time: "The neighbourhood has changed a lot."
For unfinished time: "We have planted 47 trees this term." (the term is not over yet)
grammar.commonMistake: Use the correct helper and the past participle. "She have completed her painting" is wrong; write "She has completed her painting." Never leave the participle unfinished, as in "They have flourish."
grammar.memoryTip: The present perfect is a bridge from the past to now: have or has is the bridge, and the past participle (planted, spoken, built) is the action that reaches the present.
grammar.practice:
Part A: put each verb into the present perfect. (1) She ___ (visit) the gallery three times. (2) We ___ (not see) the finished mural yet. (3) The school ___ (plant) over one hundred trees. Part B: write two sentences about things your class has done this term, using the present perfect.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: (1) has visited (2) have not seen / haven't seen (3) has planted.
Part B: open-ended — self-check model: "Our class has painted a mural for the school garden."; "We have collected recycling all term." Check that each sentence uses has/have + past participle.

grammar.title: Putting It All Together
grammar.explanation: In real English writing and speaking, we combine many grammar features in the same text. This lesson helps you practise using indefinite pronouns, adjective order, and the present perfect tense together — just as you will in the Writing Workshop.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Example paragraph:
Read this paragraph and notice the grammar features:
"Our school has started a recycling project this term. Everyone in Year 6 has collected plastic bottles and old newspapers. Someone donated a beautiful large wooden box to store the materials. We have already made three small colourful recycled sculptures for the school garden. Nobody expected the project to grow so quickly. Now anyone who visits our school can see something amazing — art made from things that people once threw away."
In this paragraph, find:
Three indefinite pronouns and their group (some-, any-, every-, no-).
Two examples of adjective order (list the adjectives and their categories).
Two sentences using the present perfect tense.
grammar.commonMistake: When you combine features, do not drop agreement. "Everyone have finished their murals" mixes a singular pronoun with a plural verb; write "Everyone has finished their murals."
grammar.memoryTip: Build one sentence at a time: choose your pronoun, order your adjectives, then check each verb. Read the paragraph aloud to hear whether it flows.
grammar.practice:
Part A: in the model paragraph, find three indefinite pronouns, two phrases with ordered adjectives, and two present perfect verbs. Part B: write a six-sentence paragraph about a school project that uses at least three indefinite pronouns, two ordered-adjective phrases, and two present perfect verbs.

=== Answer Key ===
Part A: Indefinite pronouns (any three): Everyone (every-), Someone (some-), Nobody (no-), anyone (any-), something (some-). Adjective-order phrases (any two): "a beautiful large wooden box" (opinion, size, material) and "three small colourful recycled sculptures" (quantity, size, colour, material). Present perfect verbs (any two): "has started", "has collected", "have already made".
Part B: open-ended — self-check model paragraph: "Our class has begun a new mural project. Everyone in the group has chosen a colour to paint. Someone found three large wooden panels behind the hall. We have already sketched a beautiful traditional design on the first panel. Nobody wants to stop before it is finished. Anyone who walks past can already see something amazing taking shape." Check your paragraph has at least three indefinite pronouns, two ordered-adjective phrases, and two present perfect verbs.

grammar.explanation: Strong writers apply unit grammar while revising complete paragraphs for meaning, accuracy and flow.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Read a paragraph aloud. Check sentence completeness, agreement, tense, joining words and punctuation. Revise one feature at a time.

This task uses your own three-paragraph response, so there is no single correct answer. Use this model edit to check your work:
Before: "Everyone in our class are working on the mural project. Somebody have collect a wooden large box for supplies. Nobody know when it will be finish."
After: "Everyone in our class is working on the mural project. Somebody has collected a large wooden box for supplies. Nobody knows when it will be finished."
Changes and why they help: (1) "are" -> "is" — the indefinite pronoun "Everyone" is singular, so it needs a singular verb. (3) "wooden large" -> "large wooden" — adjective order should follow size before material (OSASCOMP). grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "Amazing Arts" on their own — new words, a grammar focus, and a set of longer readings. This guide shows you what they are working on so you can talk about it with them.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 10-11 years old and works through this unit largely on their own — reading, practising and checking answers at their own pace. Your role is different from the early grades: you keep them company from outside the screen rather than leading each page.

The most useful things you can do are also the simplest: ask what the unit's texts are about, listen to them read a paragraph aloud, hear the new words used in sentences, and read their writing when they submit it. A few minutes of real conversation about the unit turns silent screen work into language they can actually use.

This guide tells you what the unit covers so you can ask good questions without working through the pages yourself.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
At this age your child can use the AI Tutor on their own — it is worth sitting in occasionally to see how they use it, and showing them what it can do.

Suggest they ask it to quiz them on this unit's words: "Ask me questions about the word 'deforestation'."

Suggest they paste in a sentence of their own and ask whether it sounds natural, and how to say it better.

Encourage 'why' questions — why a comma goes there, why the text says it that way. Asking the tutor to explain, not just to check, is where the learning is.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for supporting this unit
sections.body:
Short, regular sessions still beat one long one. A unit spread over several days sticks; a unit crammed in one sitting does not.

Talk about the reading away from the screen — over a meal, in the car. Retelling a text in their own words is one of the strongest checks of understanding there is.

Treat their writing as a draft to improve, not an answer to mark. Pick one thing to praise and one thing to sharpen, and stop there.

Praise precision and persistence, not just speed. At this stage careful, complete answers matter more than quick ones.

sections.title: How to Support This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
A simple shape for staying involved without taking over:

1. Before they start (2 min)
Skim this guide's word list and text titles so you know what to ask about later. You do not need to work through the pages yourself.

2. While they work
Let them work alone at their own pace. Be within reach for a word or an instruction they cannot crack, but resist doing the thinking for them.

3. Talk about the reading (5 min)
Ask them to tell you what "How Art Transforms a Community" was about in their own words, and what happened in "The Children of Wind Valley, part 1" — and what they thought of it.

4. Hear the words (5 min)
Pick a few words from the list below and ask for each one in a spoken sentence of their own. Saying a word out loud fixes it far better than reading it silently.

5. Check the grammar landed (3 min)
Ask them to explain "Indefinite Pronouns — The Basics" to you as if you were the student. Teaching it back is the quickest way to find out whether it stuck.

6. Read their writing (5 min)
When the Writing section is submitted, read it together. Praise one specific thing, suggest one improvement, and leave it there.
